name: Ossuary Gate
classification: primordial matter deposit from the early universe

detectability.signature: Faint thermal emission in the microwave band consistent with cosmic background radiation but at significantly elevated intensity, paired with anomalous mass readings from material that does not correspond to any element on the periodic table

proximity: Mass-density scanners return readings for material compositions that do not exist in current physics, causing diagnostic false positives
A faint but measurable thermal gradient radiates outward from the ring, detectable as a slight warming on hull sensors
contact: Physical interaction with proto-matter triggers unpredictable nucleosynthetic reactions, converting the material into conventional elements with significant energy release
Instruments in direct contact with samples undergo molecular contamination as proto-matter partially bonds with standard materials in novel configurations
The thermal output of disturbed proto-matter can spike to dangerous levels before stabilizing into its new elemental form
prolonged_exposure: Cumulative molecular contamination from ambient proto-matter particles degrades hull coatings and sensor surfaces over weeks of continuous exposure
Crew members working with proto-matter samples report persistent low-grade headaches attributed to the anomalous thermal and radiation environment
Long-term presence within the ring structure necessitates regular decontamination cycles to prevent proto-matter particulate buildup in air filtration systems

age: Approximately 13.7 billion years, dating to the first minutes after the Big Bang before nucleosynthesis was complete

behavior.cycle: The ring structure orbits a gravitational center that contains no visible mass, completing one rotation approximately every 4,200 standard years

phenomena: The proto-matter forms a toroidal ring roughly 540,000 kilometers in major radius, composed of dense nodules and filaments of material that predates the formation of conventional elements

When disturbed, proto-matter undergoes rapid nucleosynthesis, condensing into familiar elements in a process that recapitulates in seconds what originally took minutes in the primordial universe, often producing rare heavy elements in unusual abundance
The ring orbits an empty gravitational focus, suggesting the original anchoring mass has been removed or has decayed, leaving only its gravitational imprint
The proto-matter emits thermal radiation at a temperature slightly above the cosmic microwave background, as though it retains a fading memory of the heat of creation
hazards: Uncontrolled nucleosynthetic reactions from disturbed proto-matter can release dangerous levels of energy and radiation
Molecular contamination from proto-matter particulates can compromise hull integrity and sensitive equipment over extended exposure
The nature of the absent central mass is unknown, and the possibility that it could return or reactivate cannot be excluded
opportunities: Proto-matter nucleosynthesis produces heavy and rare elements on demand, potentially revolutionizing materials science and manufacturing
The deposit represents a direct physical sample of the early universe, offering observational data on conditions that existed 13.7 billion years ago
The gravitational imprint at the ring's center may preserve information about a form of matter or energy that no longer exists in the current epoch
known_incidents: A mining consortium's attempt to harvest proto-matter in bulk in 3199 triggered a cascading nucleosynthetic chain reaction that converted a 200-kilometer section of the ring into a cloud of heavy elements, releasing enough energy to destroy two extraction platforms and irradiate a third beyond salvage

The xenoarchaeological survey vessel Bone Reader recovered a proto-matter sample in 3186 that spontaneously nucleosynthesized into an isotope of an element not yet produced in any laboratory, prompting a reclassification of the periodic table
description: Ossuary Gate is a ring of primordial matter suspended in the void, a remnant of the universe's first moments preserved across nearly fourteen billion years by circumstances that cosmologists are still struggling to explain. The ring is faintly visible in the microwave band as a warm, toroidal structure roughly 540,000 kilometers in major radius, its surface composed of dense nodules and filaments of material that never completed the nucleosynthetic processes that forged the elements of the modern universe. It orbits, slowly and patiently, around a gravitational center that contains nothing at all.

The proto-matter that composes the ring is not any element. It is what elements were before they became themselves, a dense, energetic substrate that, when disturbed, undergoes rapid nucleosynthesis, condensing into familiar atoms in a violent recapitulation of the Big Bang's opening minutes. The process is unpredictable. A gentle touch might produce iron. A sharp impact might yield plutonium, or something heavier, or something that should not exist at all. The energy released scales with the amount of material disturbed, and industrial-scale extraction has proven spectacularly dangerous.

The name Ossuary Gate was given by Dr. Constance Moray, who led the first survey in 3182 and described the ring as a reliquary of the universe's bones, a gate built from the remains of creation's first and only attempt at matter before the laws of physics settled into their current form. The metaphor captured the imagination of the scientific community and the public alike. The empty gravitational focus at the ring's center has attracted particular fascination, as it implies the former presence of an anchoring mass of extraordinary density that has since vanished, leaving only its gravitational shadow.

Ossuary Gate is currently designated a protected scientific site with restricted access, though enforcement is complicated by the ring's immense size and the considerable economic incentive to harvest its materials. The catastrophic mining incident of 3199 has dampened commercial enthusiasm somewhat, but not eliminated it. A permanent research station, Reliquary Post, orbits just outside the ring and conducts ongoing studies of the proto-matter's composition and the empty gravitational focus. The most provocative finding to date is that the focus appears to be slowly weakening, raising the possibility that within a few hundred thousand years, the ring will lose its orbital anchor and begin to disperse, scattering the universe's oldest matter into the void like ashes from an urn.
